claim: PCH1 (At2g16365.2) was repeatedly co-purified with the Evening Complex (EC) by tandem affinity-purification coupled with mass spectrometry (AP-MS) analyses.
source: A protein encoded by At2g16365, a gene that was described as required for transcriptional responses to lincomycin-induced chloroplast damage (Ruckle et al., 2012), was repeatedly co-purified with the EC by tandem affinity-purification coupled with mass spectrometry (AP-MS) analyses (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work (Huang et al., 2015) and experimental data from AP-MS analyses.

claim: At2g16365 has four splice variants encoding different protein products, three of which contain an F-box domain (At2g16365.1, 3 and 4).
source: According to the TAIR10 database (Lamesch et al., 2011), At2g16365 has four splice variants encoding different protein products, three of which contain an F-box domain (At2g16365.1, 3 and 4) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to the TAIR10 database and a figure showing the splice variants.

claim: All peptides from AT2G16365 that co-purified with the EC were mapped to At2g16365.2.
source: All peptides from AT2G16365 that co-purified with the EC were mapped to At2g16365.2 (Figure 1—supplement 2 and Huang et al., 2015), which contains the first two exons and lacks the sequence encoding the F-box domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry peptide mapping and citation to previous work.

claim: Only At2g16365.2 is transcribed.
source: Semi-quantitative RT-PCR analysis and RNA-seq reads from a publically available RNA-seq dataset (Gulledge et al., 2014) indicated that only At2g16365.2 is transcribed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental RT-PCR data and RNA-seq data from a cited dataset.

claim: A T-DNA insertion loss-of-function line in At2g16365 (SALK_024229) resulted in a short-day-specific hypocotyl phenotype.
source: Furthermore, a T-DNA insertion loss-of-function line in At2g16365 (SALK_024229, Ruckle et al., 2012) resulted in a short-day-specific hypocotyl phenotype (described below).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental phenotypic data and citation to the mutant line.

claim: The At2g16365 gene was renamed PHOTOPERIODIC CONTROL OF HYPOCOTYL 1 (PCH1).
source: Thus, the At2g16365 gene was renamed PHOTOPERIODIC CONTROL OF HYPOCOTYL 1 (PCH1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the naming of the gene.

claim: PCH1 expression cycled with a peak of expression occurring in the evening under long day, 12L:12D and short day conditions.
source: Examination of microarray data from long day, 12L:12D and short day time courses (Light: Dark hours = 16:8, 12:12 and 8:16, respectively) from the DIURNAL database (Michael et al., 2008b; Mockler et al., 2007) found that expression of PCH1 cycled with a peak of expression occurring in the evening.
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data from a cited database.

claim: PCH1 mRNA accumulates after dawn, reaches a maximum at Zeitgeber time 8 (ZT8) and decreases towards the end of night.
source: PCH1 mRNA accumulates after dawn, reaches a maximum at Zeitgeber time 8 (ZT8) and decreases towards the end of night (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The PCH1 expression pattern was validated by quantitative PCR (qPCR) analyses using cDNA samples of short-day grown seedlings.
source: This expression pattern was validated by quantitative PCR (qPCR) analyses using cDNA samples of short-day grown seedlings (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The PCH1-His6-FLAG3 fusion protein accumulates after dawn, reaches a peak level in the early evening (ZT9) and a trough at subjective dawn.
source: The PCH1-His6-FLAG3 fusion protein accumulates after dawn, reaches a peak level in the early evening (ZT9) and a trough at subjective dawn (Figure 1C), similar to PCH1 expression (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Under 12L:12D and long day conditions, PCH1-His6-FLAG3 in PCH1p::PCH1 plants continues to peak near the dusk transition.
source: Under 12L:12D and long day conditions, PCH1-His6-FLAG3 in PCH1p::PCH1 plants continues to peak near the dusk transition (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: In a PCH1 constitutive expression line (PCH1ox3), PCH1 protein levels were constant under all photoperiods, unlike PCH1p::PCH1.
source: In a PCH1 constitutive expression line (PCH1ox3), PCH1 protein levels were constant under all photoperiods, unlike PCH1p::PCH1 (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Pairwise alignments of Arabidopsis PCH1 with orthologs from Oryza sativa, Brachypodium distachyon, and Populus trichocarpa indicate percent identity is 19.6%, 20.81% and 32.03%, respectively.
source: Pairwise alignments of Arabidopsis PCH1 with orthologs from Oryza sativa, Brachypodium distachyon, and Populus trichocarpa indicate percent identity is 19.6%, 20.81% and 32.03%, respectively (Clustal Omega, http://www.ebi.ac.uk/Tools/msa/clustalo/).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis using Clustal Omega.

claim: The last 43 amino acids of the C-terminus are highly conserved among PCH1 orthologs.
source: The last 43 amino acids of the C-terminus are highly conserved among PCH1 orthologs (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: PCH1 orthologs share the evening-phased expression pattern under 12L:12D.
source: In addition, PCH1 orthologs share the evening-phased expression pattern under 12L:12D (Figure 1D), suggesting that PCH1 may have conserved time-of-day-specific functions (Michael et al., 2008a).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1D and inference from the data.

claim: Unlike phyB-9, elf3-2 and elf4-2, which exhibit longer hypocotyls than wild type under all photoperiods tested, pch1 shows a day-length-specific defect.
source: Unlike phyB-9, elf3-2 and elf4-2, which exhibit longer hypocotyls than wild type under all photoperiods tested, pch1 shows a day-length-specific defect (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under long days, hypocotyls of pch1 are not longer than wild type.
source: Under long days, hypocotyls of pch1 are not longer than wild type (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: As the dark period extended to 12 hr, pch1 exhibited a slightly but significantly longer hypocotyl than wild type (p<0.01).
source: As the dark period extended to 12 hr, pch1 exhibited a slightly but significantly longer hypocotyl than wild type (p<0.01) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under short days, pch1 mutants elongated hypocotyls even further (p<0.0001).
source: Under short days, pch1 mutants elongated hypocotyls even further (p<0.0001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Constitutive expression of PCH1 resulted in the opposite phenotype: PCH1ox3 mutants have shorter hypocotyls than wild type under all photoperiods (p<0.0001).
source: Constitutive expression of PCH1 resulted in the opposite phenotype: PCH1ox3 mutants have shorter hypocotyls than wild type under all photoperiods (p<0.0001) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PCH1p::PCH1 rescued the hypocotyl length phenotype of pch1 mutants in two independent lines.
source: PCH1p::PCH1 rescued the hypocotyl length phenotype of pch1 mutants in two independent lines (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), showing that the level and/or timing of PCH1 expression is critical for proper regulation of hypocotyl elongation.
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and inference from the rescue experiment.

claim: Wild type plants showed rhythmic hypocotyl growth under short days, with a maximal growth rate at dawn.
source: Wild type plants showed rhythmic hypocotyl growth under short days, with a maximal growth rate at dawn, as described (Nozue et al., 2007) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and citation to previous work.

claim: On the third night post-germination (from ZT56 to ZT72), pch1 seedlings had higher hypocotyl growth rates than wild type during the night, especially during the 3rd to the 5th night.
source: On the third night post-germination (from ZT56 to ZT72), pch1 seedlings had higher hypocotyl growth rates than wild type during the night, especially during the 3rd to the 5th night (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Constitutive expression of PCH1 in PCH1ox3 inhibited hypocotyl elongation throughout the night.
source: Supporting the hypothesis that PCH1 is a suppressor of hypocotyl elongation, constitutive expression of PCH1 in PCH1ox3 inhibited hypocotyl elongation throughout the night, while PCH1p::PCH1 restored the growth rate to wild type levels (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The luciferase activity of CCA1::LUC in wild type, pch1 and PCH1ox3 oscillates with a period of ~24 hr (23.20 ± 0.45, 23.13 ± 0.37, and 22.97 ± 0.32 hr, respectively, mean ± SD, n = 8).
source: The luciferase activity of CCA1::LUC in wild type, pch1 and PCH1ox3 oscillates with a period of ~24 hr (23.20 ± 0.45, 23.13 ± 0.37, and 22.97 ± 0.32 hr, respectively, mean ± SD, n = 8) (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), showing that PCH1 levels do not affect the circadian period of the reporter.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter data shown in Figure 3A, B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCH1 levels do not affect the circadian period of the CCA1::LUC reporter.
source: The luciferase activity of CCA1::LUC in wild type, pch1 and PCH1ox3 oscillates with a period of ~24 hr (23.20 ± 0.45, 23.13 ± 0.37, and 22.97 ± 0.32 hr, respectively, mean ± SD, n = 8) (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), showing that PCH1 levels do not affect the circadian period of the reporter.
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase reporter data and inference from the results.

claim: The pch1 mutation results in an early flowering phenotype under long days.
source: However, the pch1 mutation results in an early flowering phenotype under long days, while PCH1ox3 flowers later than wild type (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PCH1ox3 flowers later than wild type under long days.
source: However, the pch1 mutation results in an early flowering phenotype under long days, while PCH1ox3 flowers later than wild type (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The flowering time of pch1 or PCH1ox3 is not different from wild type under short days.
source: Unlike elf4-2 plants, which flower early under both long days and short days (Doyle et al., 2002), the flowering time of pch1 or PCH1ox3 is not different from wild type under short days (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 3D and citation to previous work.

claim: PCH1 is an output rather than a component of the circadian clock.
source: Together, the results show that PCH1 is an output rather than a component of the circadian clock and that the pch1 mutant is still sensitive to photoperiod in respect to flowering control.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the circadian and flowering time data.

claim: The pch1 mutant is still sensitive to photoperiod in respect to flowering control.
source: Together, the results show that PCH1 is an output rather than a component of the circadian clock and that the pch1 mutant is still sensitive to photoperiod in respect to flowering control.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the flowering time data under different photoperiods.

claim: PCH1 AP-MS identified 17 proteins from three biological replicate purifications after excluding non-specific binding proteins.
source: After excluding non-specific binding proteins from negative control GFP-His6-FLAG3 AP-MS and non-specific structural, metabolic, and photosynthetic proteins (Huang et al., 2015; Mellacheruvu et al., 2013), PCH1 AP-MS identified 17 proteins from three biological replicate purifications (Table 1, for all co-purified proteins, see Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data shown in Table 1 and citation to methods.

claim: 15 of the 17 proteins that co-precipitated with PCH1 overlap with the ELF3 AP-MS.
source: 15 of the 17 proteins that co-precipitated with PCH1 overlap with the ELF3 AP-MS (Huang et al., 2015), including the EC components ELF3, ELF4, and LUX, all five phytochromes (A to E), TANDEM ZINC KNUCKLE/PLUS3 (TZP), DAYSLEEPER, MUT9-LIKE KINASE 2 (MLK2), CHLOROPLAST RNA BINDING (CRB), the protease RD21a, and the COP1-SPA1 complex (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data shown in Table 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: COP1-SPA1 is part of a complex that mediates the light-dependent turnover of light signaling components.
source: COP1-SPA1 is part of a complex that mediates the light-dependent turnover of light signaling components (Saijo et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TZP positively regulates morning-specific plant growth and flowering responses through associating with phyB.
source: TZP positively regulates morning-specific plant growth and flowering responses through associating with phyB (Kaiserli et al., 2015; Loudet et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DAYSLEEPER is a hAT transposase that is required for proper embryonic development.
source: DAYSLEEPER is a hAT transposase that is required for proper embryonic development (Bundock and Hooykaas, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MLK2 is a nuclear kinase that regulates circadian rhythms and osmotic stress responses.
source: MLK2 is a nuclear kinase that regulates circadian rhythms and osmotic stress responses (Huang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CRB is a RNA binding protein that regulates circadian rhythms.
source: CRB is a RNA binding protein that regulates circadian rhythms (Hassidim et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: RD21a is a drought-inducible cysteine protease.
source: RD21a is a drought-inducible cysteine protease (Koizumi et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and TOPLESS (TPL) were proteins co-purified with PCH1 that were not identified in ELF3 AP-MS.
source: FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and TOPLESS (TPL) were proteins co-purified with PCH1 that were not identified in ELF3 AP-MS.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of AP-MS data.

claim: FHY1 interacts with phyA and is required for phyA nuclear import upon light treatment.
source: FHY1 interacts with phyA and is required for phyA nuclear import upon light treatment (Hiltbrunner et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TPL is a Groucho/Tup1-type transcriptional co-repressor that interacts with proteins from circadian and development pathways.
source: TPL is a Groucho/Tup1-type transcriptional co-repressor that interacts with proteins from circadian and development pathways (Liu and Karmarkar, 2008; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PCH1 is a component of a protein-protein interaction network consisting of the EC, phytochromes and the COP1-SPA1 complex.
source: In summary, our PCH1 AP-MS results confirm that PCH1 is a component of a reported protein-protein interaction network consisting of the EC, phytochromes and the COP1-SPA1 complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the AP-MS data.

claim: ELF3 and ELF4 are dispensable for PCH1 to associate with the light signaling components in the network.
source: Although PCH1 was originally found co-precipitating with ELF4 and ELF3, both are dispensable for PCH1 to associate with the light signaling components in the network (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data in different genetic backgrounds shown in Table 2.

claim: phyB is critical for recruiting PCH1 to the EC-phytochrome-COP1 interactome.
source: In comparison, phyB is critical for recruiting PCH1 to the EC-phytochrome-COP1 interactome.
evidence: The claim is inferred from AP-MS data in phyB-9 background.

claim: In phyB-9, PCH1 AP-MS did not co-precipitate the EC, the COP1-SPA1 complex, TZP, MLK2, RD21a, TPL, or phyC.
source: In phyB-9, PCH1AP-MS did not co-precipitate the EC, the COP1-SPA1 complex, TZP, MLK2, RD21a, TPL, or phyC (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data in phyB-9 background shown in Table 1.

claim: The association of PCH1 with DAYSLEEPER, CRB, phyD, phyE, phyA, and FHY1 was retained in phyB-9.
source: However, the association with DAYSLEEPER, CRB, phyD, phyE, phyA, and FHY1 was retained in phyB-9.
evidence: The claim is supported by AP-MS data in phyB-9 background.

claim: The association of PCH1 with the EC, the COP1-SPA1 complex, MLK2, and TZP is bridged by phyB.
source: Therefore, our PCH1 AP-MS analysis in phyB-9 suggests that the association of PCH1 with the EC, the COP1-SPA1 complex, MLK2, and TZP is bridged by phyB, while loss of phyC could be due to a reduction in phyC caused by the phyB mutation (Clack et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from AP-MS data in phyB-9 background and citation to previous work.

claim: PCH1 is integrated into the EC-phytochrome-COP1 interactome in vivo through the association with phyB.
source: Together, our PCH1 AP-MS analyses in different genetic backgrounds demonstrate that PCH1 is integrated into the EC-phytochrome-COP1 interactome in vivo through the association with phyB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from AP-MS data in different genetic backgrounds.

claim: PCH1 directly interacts with the C-terminus of phyB in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Consistent with the AP-MS data, direct interactions between PCH1 and ELF3, ELF4, LUX, COP1 or TZP were not observed (Figure 4A). However, PCH1 interacted with the C-terminus of phyB (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PCH1 interacted with the C-terminal tail of phyD and phyE, but not with either phyA or phyC in yeast.
source: PCH1 also interacted with the C-terminal tail of phyD and phyE, but not with either phyA or phyC in yeast (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: phyB-GFP specifically co-precipitated with PCH1-His6-FLAG3 in an anti-FLAG immunoprecipitation in tobacco leaves.
source: To validate the PCH1-phyB interaction in planta, PCH1-His6-FLAG3 was transiently co-expressed with a phyB-GFP fusion protein in tobacco (Nicotiana benthamiana) leaves. phyB-GFP specifically co-precipitated with PCH1-His6-FLAG3 in an anti-FLAG immunoprecipitation, while PCH1 and GFP alone did not interact (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Endogenous phyB co-precipitated with PCH1 at the end of the light treatment (ZT12).
source: Endogenous phyB co-precipitated with PCH1 at the end of the light treatment (ZT12), confirming the AP-MS results (Figure 4D, lane 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Less phyB was co-precipitated with PCH1-His6-FLAG3 under extended dark periods (24 or 48 hr in dark), although the levels of phyB in the input were increased in these conditions.
source: Less phyB was co-precipitated with PCH1-His6-FLAG3 under extended dark periods (24 or 48 hr in dark, lane 4 and 5), although the levels of phyB in the input were increased in these conditions, indicating that light promotes the PCH1-phyB interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D and inference from the results.

claim: Light promotes the PCH1-phyB interaction.
source: Less phyB was co-precipitated with PCH1-His6-FLAG3 under extended dark periods (24 or 48 hr in dark, lane 4 and 5), although the levels of phyB in the input were increased in these conditions, indicating that light promotes the PCH1-phyB interaction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data under different light conditions.

claim: 12 hr of red light treatment on the last day was sufficient to maintain the PCH1-phyB interaction.
source: The red-light sensitivity of the PCH1-phyB interaction was tested and found that 12 hr of red light treatment on the last day was sufficient to maintain the PCH1-phyB interaction (Figure 4D, lane 6), suggesting that PCH1 bound to the active Pfr form of phyB.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D and inference from the results.

claim: PCH1 bound to the active Pfr form of phyB.
source: The red-light sensitivity of the PCH1-phyB interaction was tested and found that 12 hr of red light treatment on the last day was sufficient to maintain the PCH1-phyB interaction (Figure 4D, lane 6), suggesting that PCH1 bound to the active Pfr form of phyB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data under red light conditions.

claim: A ten-minute pulse of far-red light at the end of day (EOD-FRp) that converted phyB to the inactive Pr form reduced the PCH1-phyB interaction.
source: Conversely, a ten-minute pulse of far-red light at the end of day (EOD-FRp) that converted phyB to the inactive Pr form reduced the PCH1-phyB interaction (Figure 4D, lane 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PCH1 weakly interacts with either the apoprotein or the Pr form of phyB but preferentially binds the active Pfr form of phyB.
source: PCH1 weakly interacts with either the apoprotein or the Pr form of phyB but preferentially binds the active Pfr form of phyB, compared to the YPet (a YFP variant) control (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PCH1 directly interacts with phyB, and the interaction is light- and wavelength-sensitive in vivo and in vitro.
source: In summary, PCH1 directly interacts with phyB, and the interaction is light- and wavelength-sensitive in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro binding assay data.

claim: PCH1 is a new phyB-interacting protein and is integrated into the EC-phytochrome-COP1 interactome in vivo through the association with phyB.
source: Combined with our PCH1 AP-MS analyses in different genetic backgrounds, our protein-protein interaction/association data demonstrate that PCH1 is a new phyB-interacting protein and is integrated into the EC-phytochrome-COP1 interactome in vivo through the association with phyB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from AP-MS and protein-protein interaction data.

claim: A subcellular localization tool identified a bipartite nuclear localization signal in PCH1.
source: A subcellular localization tool (Kosugi et al., 2009) identified a bipartite nuclear localization signal in PCH1 (highlighted in Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational prediction and reference to a figure.

claim: PCH1 was exclusively localized in the nucleus when transiently expressed in tobacco.
source: Transient expression of a PCH1-YPet fusion in tobacco showed that PCH1 was exclusively localized in the nucleus, while the YPet control was localized to both nucleus and cytoplasm (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PCH1-YPet was localized to subnuclear foci similar to the photobodies that phytochromes form after light exposure.
source: Furthermore, PCH1-YPet was localized to subnuclear foci (Figure 5A) similar to the photobodies that phytochromes form after light exposure (Kircher et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and citation to previous work.

claim: When PCH1-YPet and phyB-CFP were co-expressed, they co-localized into nuclear photobodies.
source: Indeed, when PCH1-YPet and phyB-CFP were co-expressed, they co-localized into nuclear photobodies (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of PCH1 severely attenuated formation of large photobodies, particularly at low fluence red light.
source: We found that loss of PCH1 severely attenuated formation of large photobodies, particularly at low fluence red light (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In both low and high red-light conditions, pch1 mutants had more small photobodies.
source: In both low and high red-light conditions, pch1 mutants had more small photobodies, suggesting that PCH1 regulates either the transition from small to large photobody or the maintenance of large photobodies.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data and inference from the results.

claim: PCH1 regulates either the transition from small to large photobody or the maintenance of large photobodies.
source: In both low and high red-light conditions, pch1 mutants had more small photobodies, suggesting that PCH1 regulates either the transition from small to large photobody or the maintenance of large photobodies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from confocal microscopy data.

claim: The phenotypes of pch1 mutants are distinct from mutations in HEMERA, which is necessary for photobody initiation.
source: The phenotypes of pch1 mutants are distinct from mutations in HEMERA, which is necessary for photobody initiation (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous work and citation.

claim: Constitutive overexpression of PCH1 resulted in an increase in the number and prolonged maintenance of large photobodies during the night at both high and low light intensity compared to wild type.
source: Conversely, constitutive overexpression of PCH1 resulted in an increase in the number and prolonged maintenance of large photobodies during the night at both high and low light intensity compared to wild type (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Altering PCH1 levels does not induce a constitutively photomorphogenic phenotype.
source: Altering PCH1 levels, however, does not induce a constitutively photomorphogenic phenotype (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of PCH1 to phyB after light exposure traps phyB in an active conformation and prolongs phyB localization to large photobodies.
source: We favor a model wherein binding of PCH1 to phyB after light exposure traps phyB in an active conformation and prolongs phyB localization to large photobodies by either slowing dark reversion rates or through maintaining the superstructure of the photobody once formed.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: pch1 seedlings have longer hypocotyls and are hyposensitive to red-light-mediated suppression of hypocotyl elongation compared with wild type.
source: Compared with wild type, pch1 seedlings have longer hypocotyls and are hyposensitive to red-light-mediated suppression of hypocotyl elongation. This phenotype was rescued in PCH1p::PCH1 transgenic plants (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PCH1ox3 plants showed hypersensitivity to red light under all light fluences.
source: Conversely, PCH1ox3 plants showed hypersensitivity to red light under all light fluences (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In either constant far-red or blue light, hypocotyl lengths of pch1 and PCHox3 seedlings resembled those of wild type plants.
source: In either constant far-red or blue light, hypocotyl lengths of pch1 and PCHox3 seedlings resembled those of wild type plants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by hypocotyl measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCH1 specifically modulates hypocotyl elongation in response to red light.
source: These data suggest that PCH1 specifically modulates hypocotyl elongation in response to red light.
evidence: The claim is inferred from hypocotyl measurement data under different light conditions.

claim: In wild type, transcripts of HFR1 and ATHB-2 are suppressed by daylight and accumulate in the evening, with a peak at dawn.
source: In wild type, transcripts of HFR1 and ATHB-2 are suppressed by daylight and accumulate in the evening, with a peak at dawn (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: pch1 mutants up-regulated HFR1 and ATHB-2 during the dark period.
source: pch1 mutants up-regulated HFR1 and ATHB-2 during the dark period, in agreement with our growth rate data showing the acceleration of hypocotyl growth in pch1 during night (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Overexpression of PCH1 suppresses HFR1 and ATHB-2 transcript levels throughout the light/dark cycle.
source: Conversely, overexpression of PCH1 suppresses HFR1 and ATHB-2 transcript levels throughout the light/dark cycle (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Phytochrome photoperception and downstream gene expression is regulated by PCH1.
source: These data demonstrate that phytochrome photoperception and downstream gene expression is regulated by PCH1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from gene expression data.

claim: PIF4 mRNA levels were upregulated in pch1 compared to wild type in a qPCR assay.
source: PIF4 mRNA levels were upregulated in pch1 compared to wild type in a qPCR assay (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Higher PIF4 levels were observed in the evening in pch1 compared to wild type.
source: Using a pif4/PIF4p::PIF4-HA line to detect PIF4 protein levels, we observed higher PIF4 levels in the evening in pch1 compared to wild type (Figure 7B), suggesting that PCH1 can modulate PIF4 levels in the early evening.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B and inference from the results.

claim: PCH1 can modulate PIF4 levels in the early evening.
source: Using a pif4/PIF4p::PIF4-HA line to detect PIF4 protein levels, we observed higher PIF4 levels in the evening in pch1 compared to wild type (Figure 7B), suggesting that PCH1 can modulate PIF4 levels in the early evening.
evidence: The claim is inferred from western blot data.

claim: Introducing pif mutant alleles into the pch1 mutant background progressively ameliorated the elongated hypocotyl phenotype of the pch1 mutant.
source: Introducing pif mutant alleles into the pch1 mutant background progressively ameliorated the elongated hypocotyl phenotype of the pch1 mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data.

claim: Altered PIF levels underlie the growth defects seen in pch1.
source: Taken together, these results show that altered PIF levels underlie the growth defects seen in pch1, and that PIF3, 4, and 5 are required for the hypocotyl growth defects in pch1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic interaction and gene expression data.

claim: PIF3, 4, and 5 are required for the hypocotyl growth defects in pch1.
source: Taken together, these results show that altered PIF levels underlie the growth defects seen in pch1, and that PIF3, 4, and 5 are required for the hypocotyl growth defects in pch1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic interaction data.

claim: PCH1 is a new factor that regulates photoperiod-responsive growth by integrating the clock with light perception pathways through modulating daily phyB-signaling.
source: Thus, PCH1 is a new factor that regulates photoperiod-responsive growth by integrating the clock with light perception pathways through modulating daily phyB-signaling.
evidence: This is a summary claim inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: PCH1 is a new phytochrome interacting protein that functions to increase sensitivity to red light and prolongs phyB activity by maintaining photobody formation.
source: Here we show that PCH1 is a new phytochrome interacting protein that functions to increase sensitivity to red light and prolongs phyB activity by maintaining photobody formation.
evidence: This is a summary claim inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: PCH1 binding to the C-terminus of phyB likely stabilizes the Pfr conformer.
source: PCH1 binding to the C-terminus of phyB likely stabilizes the Pfr conformer (Chen et al., 2005), thereby providing a molecular memory of light exposure to prevent inappropriate elongation in response to long nights.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: Recent models of phyB signaling and photoconversion postulated that specific binding of a yet identified factor to phyB in the Pfr state might prevent dark-reversion and maintain phyB to photobodies to sustain an active pool of phyB in the dark in vivo.
source: Recent models of phyB signaling and photoconversion postulated that specific binding of a yet identified factor to phyB in the Pfr state might prevent dark-reversion and maintain phyB to photobodies to sustain an active pool of phyB in the dark in vivo (Klose et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim from previous modeling work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The short day-specific phenotype of pch1 results from the coincidence of the internal clock-controlled oscillation of PCH1 and PIF4, and external photoperiodic cues.
source: We propose that the short day-specific phenotype of pch1 results from the coincidence of the internal clock-controlled oscillation of PCH1 and PIF4, and external photoperiodic cues.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: In short days, PCH1 peaks at dusk, binds photoactivated phyB and prolongs phyB photobody formation to maintain phyB in the Pfr state, which then suppresses PIF4 levels in the early evening, reducing PIF4 activities and hypocotyl growth.
source: In short days, PCH1 peaks at dusk, binds photoactivated phyB and prolongs phyB photobody formation to maintain phyB in the Pfr state, which then suppresses PIF4 levels in the early evening, reducing PIF4 activities and hypocotyl growth (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 8.

claim: As the daytime increases in long days, the peak of PIF4 (at ZT8) is no longer at dusk but in the middle of the day.
source: As the daytime increases in long days, the peak of PIF4 (at ZT8) is no longer at dusk but in the middle of the day (Yamashino et al., 2014 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1), when light perception by the phytochromes would act as the major suppressor of elongation through post-translation regulation of PIF protein levels, masking the requirement of PCH1 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a claim based on expression data from a cited study and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: PCH1 overexpression lines would constantly suppress hypocotyl elongation due to maintaining phyB photobodies throughout the night, leading to shortened hypocotyls.
source: PCH1 overexpression lines would constantly suppress hypocotyl elongation due to maintaining phyB photobodies throughout the night (Figure 5B), leading to shortened hypocotyls as observed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 2A.

claim: Other PIFs (e.g. PIF3 and PIF5) also contribute to the hypocotyl phenotype of pch1.
source: It is likely other PIFs (e.g. PIF3 and PIF5) also contribute to the hypocotyl phenotype of pch1, as suggested by genetic analysis showing that higher order pif mutations progressively suppresses the long hypocotyl phenotype of pch1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic interaction data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Modulating PCH1 levels or its expression pattern could potentially alter light perception and lead to improved growth responses at latitudes where photoperiod changes during the agricultural season or in species whose yield is highly sensitive to photoperiod.
source: We anticipate that modulating PCH1 levels or its expression pattern could potentially alter light perception and lead to improved growth responses at latitudes where photoperiod changes during the agricultural season or in species whose yield is highly sensitive to photoperiod (Sadras and Slafer, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications based on the findings.
